topic: Giving feedback that lands: how a manager gives a direct report specific, timely feedback on one piece of work, so it is heard and acted on rather than defended against
scope_note: Conservative sheet for a corporate soft-skills lesson. The four moves (situation, behaviour, impact, then ask and agree a next step) are presented as common workplace practice, not as a research finding. Two research references (Kluger and DeNisi 1996; Hattie and Timperley 2007) support only the general direction that feedback aimed at the task tends to work better than feedback aimed at the person; no effect sizes or percentages are claimed. Named sources appear in reference_hint for the reviewer, not necessarily in the lesson. No HR, disciplinary or formal performance processes are covered.

facts.statement: Situation, Behaviour, Impact is a widely used workplace structure for feedback: name the situation, describe the specific behaviour, then say what it caused.
facts.reference_hint: Center for Creative Leadership, Situation-Behavior-Impact (SBI) feedback model; widely reproduced in management training material
facts.caveat: Established as a widely used practice, not as a research-proven method. The lesson may describe it as common practice; it may name the Center for Creative Leadership as its origin only if the reviewer agrees.

facts.statement: A common extension of that structure is to finish by asking for the other person's view and then agreeing a next step together, so the feedback becomes a conversation rather than a verdict.
facts.reference_hint: Center for Creative Leadership's SBI-I variant adds asking about Intent to open a two-way discussion; Stone and Heen, Thanks for the Feedback (2014)
facts.caveat: Combining the ask and the agreed next step into one fourth move is this lesson's framing of common practice, not a single named standard.

facts.statement: The situation names when and where, specifically enough that the person can picture the moment, for example the client update that went out on a particular day.
facts.reference_hint: Center for Creative Leadership, SBI model

facts.statement: The behaviour is what the person actually did or said, something another person could have seen or heard, not a guess about their attitude, intent or character.
facts.reference_hint: Center for Creative Leadership, SBI model

facts.statement: Describing behaviour and judging the person are different: saying the update did not state when the change takes effect describes the work, while calling someone careless judges them.
facts.reference_hint: Standard distinction in feedback practice; see Center for Creative Leadership, SBI model
facts.caveat: The example wording is illustrative and invented for the lesson.

facts.statement: The impact is the concrete consequence of the behaviour for the work, a client, the team or the manager, stated as what happened rather than as a verdict.
facts.reference_hint: Center for Creative Leadership, SBI model

facts.statement: Feedback does not automatically improve performance: a large review of feedback studies found that a sizeable share of feedback interventions made performance worse rather than better.
facts.reference_hint: Kluger and DeNisi (1996), 'The Effects of Feedback Interventions on Performance', Psychological Bulletin
facts.caveat: Keep the share unquantified in the lesson. The paper reports the figure, but the sheet does not carry it, so the script must not state a fraction or percentage.

facts.statement: Reviews of feedback research suggest that feedback which keeps attention on the task tends to help more than feedback which turns attention to the person and their self-image.
facts.reference_hint: Kluger and DeNisi (1996), Feedback Intervention Theory; Hattie and Timperley (2007), 'The Power of Feedback', Review of Educational Research
facts.caveat: Much of this evidence comes from laboratory and classroom settings, and effects vary widely. State it as a tendency the research points to, never as a guarantee or with an effect size.

facts.statement: A vague or judgemental verdict gives the person nothing specific to act on and is easily heard as a judgement of them, which tends to invite defending rather than discussing.
facts.reference_hint: Practitioner consensus, consistent with Kluger and DeNisi (1996) and Hattie and Timperley (2007); Stone and Heen, Thanks for the Feedback (2014), on why feedback triggers defensiveness
facts.caveat: A tendency, not a law: some people take a blunt verdict well, and a specific comment can still be defended against.

facts.statement: Common practice is to give feedback soon after the work, while both people remember it clearly, rather than saving concerns up for a later review.
facts.reference_hint: Widely taught management practice; Shute (2008), 'Focus on Formative Feedback', Review of Educational Research, on the mixed evidence about timing
facts.caveat: Research on immediate versus delayed feedback is mixed, so present this as practice. Soon means while it is fresh and at a calm, private moment, not instantly or in passing.

facts.statement: Keeping a feedback conversation to one piece of work makes it easier to hear and act on than a list of several concerns at once.
facts.caveat: Practitioner advice, not a research finding.

facts.statement: Asking for the person's view before agreeing a next step lets them add context the manager may not have, and makes the next step something they helped choose.
facts.reference_hint: Center for Creative Leadership, SBI-I (Intent); Stone and Heen, Thanks for the Feedback (2014)
facts.caveat: Present as good practice; it can still go badly if the question is not a real one.

facts.statement: A useful next step is small and concrete: what will be done differently, on what piece of work, and when the two of them will look at it again.
facts.caveat: Practitioner advice, not a research finding.

facts.statement: The same structure works for positive feedback: naming the specific behaviour and its impact tells the person exactly what to keep doing.
facts.reference_hint: Center for Creative Leadership, SBI model, which is described as working for both reinforcing and corrective feedback

facts.statement: A structure is not a script: tone, a private setting and the working relationship still shape how feedback is received, and the moves should sound like the manager, not like a form.
facts.reference_hint: Practitioner consensus; Stone and Heen, Thanks for the Feedback (2014), on relationship triggers
facts.caveat: Practitioner advice, not a research finding.

facts.statement: The four moves are a practical habit that many organisations teach, not a formula proven by research to work every time.
facts.reference_hint: No controlled studies of this exact sequence were found for this sheet; the supporting research (F7, F8) is about feedback in general
facts.caveat: The script must frame the method as common practice throughout.

not_claimed: Any fixed praise-to-criticism ratio for feedback at work (for example the so-called Losada positivity ratio, whose mathematics was challenged and formally corrected, or 'five positives for every negative').
That the feedback sandwich (praise, criticism, praise) always works or is the recommended method; it is popular, but the evidence for it is thin and it can bury the message.
That SBI or the four moves are scientifically proven, or proven to change performance by a set amount.
Any percentage of employees who want more feedback, quit because of poor feedback, or disengage after criticism; such survey figures circulate without a reviewed source here.
Any effect size or fraction from Kluger and DeNisi or Hattie and Timperley; the sheet carries only the direction of their findings.
That immediate feedback is always better than delayed feedback; the evidence on timing is mixed.
That negative feedback always demotivates, or that positive feedback always motivates.
Generational claims, such as one generation needing more feedback than another.
Communication percentage rules (the 7-38-55 split of words, tone and body language) applied to feedback; that figure comes from narrow studies of feelings and is widely misused.
That a structure guarantees the other person will not get defensive.

review.note: Written conservatively by the knowledge stage agent. Reviewer please confirm: (1) whether the lesson may name the Center for Creative Leadership as SBI's origin or keep it as 'a common practice'; (2) whether F7 and F8 (research direction, no numbers) may be voiced in the lesson or kept as background only.
